# Plants, fungi and the rest of the eukaryotes

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/03-plants-fungi-other.yml` and not yet reviewed by a
second reader.
:::

Cross-species comparison of alternative splicing has a measurement problem
sitting in front of it. Detected splicing scales with how deeply a transcriptome
was sampled, and sequencing quality and library construction differ between
projects. One early comparison reached the conclusion that it was impractical to
state the exact level of alternative splicing even in the organisms it had
itself tested [@kim2006eukaryotes]. Published prevalence figures are positions
on different saturation curves, and a bar chart that places them side by side is
comparing the experiments.

The within-study comparisons survive that objection, and they are the ones this
chapter leans on. The broadest of them covers 1,494 species using a single
per-coding-sequence transcript-count metric. Splicing is minimal in prokaryotes
and unicellular eukaryotes, highest in mammals and birds, and only moderate in
plants despite wide variation in plant genome composition
[@delafuente2025treeoflife].

## Plants {#sec-plants}

A normalised deep-coverage survey of Arabidopsis put alternative splicing at
61.2 per cent of intron-containing genes, in flower and seedling tissue grown
without stress, and those authors treat the figure as a floor
[@marquez2012arabidopsis].

### Intron retention is the commonest event {#sec-class-balance}

The flavour differs as much as the amount. Cassette exons predominate in
animals, while intron retention is the more frequent class in other taxa
[@grutzmann2013fungal]. The five event names are defined in @sec-event-classes.
Arabidopsis follows the second pattern, with intron retention the single
commonest event class in that survey, at roughly two fifths of everything the
transcript assembly detected [@marquez2012arabidopsis].

The same authors then qualified their own result. Most retained introns were
supported by far fewer reads than the junction that removes them, and about 73
per cent had a retention ratio below 1 [@marquez2012arabidopsis]. Counting
events overstates how much retained-intron RNA a plant cell is actually holding.

### Thermosensory splicing in FLM and MAF2

Flowering time in Arabidopsis is set partly by how two genes are spliced. FLM is
the better known of them, and its transcripts were cloned and sequenced at three
growth temperatures. The share of non-canonical isoforms, which mostly
carry premature stop codons, rose from 30 per cent at 16 degrees to over 50 per
cent at 27 degrees [@capovilla2017flm].

The mechanism is not the one originally proposed. CRISPR deletion of FLM exon 2
or exon 3 forced plants to make only one of the two major isoforms. Those
restricted to the warm-temperature isoform flowered early, but no earlier than
a complete FLM null. That ordering argues against a dominant-negative role
for the warm isoform. Driving the same isoform from a constitutive promoter does
produce early flowering, so the effect depends on dose
[@capovilla2017flm].

MAF2 arrived at the same trick independently. At low temperature its abundant
variant encodes a protein that partners SVP to repress flowering. Warming shifts
the balance toward an intron-retaining variant carrying a premature stop, whose
product can neither bind SVP nor repress [@airoldi2015maf2], so one gene family
evolved thermosensory splicing twice.

### COOLAIR and the clock genes

Vernalisation at the FLC locus runs through isoform choice on the antisense
strand. The cold-induced COOLAIR transcripts exist as several isoforms
distinguished by splicing and polyadenylation. The cold-specific distal class
II.ii isoform represses FLC by sequestering the activator FRIGIDA away from the
FLC promoter [@long2024coolair].

The circadian clock is spliced unproductively on purpose. A systematic survey of
Arabidopsis clock genes found unproductive splicing widespread among them,
mostly full or partial intron retention generating in-frame premature stops. The
CCA1 and LHY variants are conserved between the two paralogues, and the CCA1
event is conserved across plant phyla [@filichkin2012clock]. Barley seedlings
shifted to low temperature change the splicing of core clock genes including the
orthologues of LHY and PRR7, which puts the mechanism in a monocot crop as well
[@calixto2016barley].

### Stress responses and a shoot-to-root signal

An Arabidopsis experiment found 49.4 per cent of its intron-containing genes
alternatively spliced under salt, pooled across three salt concentrations, and a
tenth of those shifted their isoform ratio significantly with the stress
[@ding2014salt]. The figure has no companion measurement in untreated
plants, so it cannot be read as an increase. The depth usually quoted for the
study is not the depth at which its splicing was counted either. The authors
drew 18 million read pairs at random from each library first, so that every
condition was measured alike [@ding2014salt]. Maize grown through realistic daily temperature
cycles raised its splicing frequency as maximum daily temperature rose. Retained introns and skipped exons increased most, and the
splicing regulators were themselves among the genes most often affected, SR45a
among them [@li2021maize].

Light changes splicing in Arabidopsis roots, and not as a direct response to
light. The signal traces to sugars made by photosynthesis in the shoot, acting
through the TOR kinase pathway. Those authors describe it as a shoot-to-root
route coordinating splicing across the whole plant [@riegler2021light].

### Splice variants that change grain size

Two crop loci show the effect sizes involved. In tropical japonica rice, six
SNPs at the OsLG3b locus change how the OsMADS1 transcript is spliced, and that
splice variation was associated with grain length in a candidate-region
analysis [@yu2018oslg3b]. A near-isogenic line carried the large-grain donor
allele in a Nipponbare background. Its grains were 7.5 per cent longer and 3.5
per cent thicker, and yield per plant rose 7.1 per cent. Heading date, tiller
number and grains per panicle did not change significantly [@yu2018oslg3b].

Bread wheat makes five splice variants of the G-protein gamma subunit gene
TaGS3, and two of them pull in opposite directions. Overexpressing TaGS3.1 cut
grain weight by 5.89 per cent and length by 5.04 per cent. Overexpressing
TaGS3.5 raised grain weight by 5.70 per cent and length by 4.30 per cent
[@ren2021tags3]. Which isoform a plant makes is an agronomic trait, at
single-digit percentages that a breeding programme would take.

## Fungi {#sec-fungi}

Budding yeast is the organism that taught most people what splicing is, and it
is unrepresentative. Splicing is required in only about 4 per cent of
*Saccharomyces cerevisiae* protein-coding genes, and the genes that do carry an
intron are structurally plain, typically two exons and one intron. The same
reanalysis nonetheless reports pervasive use of alternative splice sites within
that small set [@schreiber2015yeast].

Some of that simplicity was acquired, in that the widely conserved alternatively
spliced gene SKI7/HBS1 was replaced in *Saccharomyces* by a pair of duplicated,
intronless genes during whole-genome doubling, converting one isoform choice
into two separate loci [@hurtig2020budding]. Gene duplication and alternative
splicing can reach the same destination.

What regulated splicing budding yeast retains is concentrated in meiosis. The
activator Mer1 is required to splice four meiosis-specific pre-mRNAs, MER2,
MER3, AMA1 and SPO22, whose introns are otherwise poor spliceosome substrates
[@venkataramanan2017meiotic]. Fission yeast runs the same logic with the sign
reversed. Mmi1 binds primary transcripts of thirty or more meiotic genes in
vegetative cells, inhibits splicing of the introns near its binding sites while
sparing distant ones, and routes the transcript to hyperadenylation-dependent
decay. At least 29 target genes are therefore transcribed constitutively and
expressed only in meiosis [@chen2011mmi1].

![Within one comparative study using one method, per-gene alternative splicing
rate tracks how multicellular the group is. Rates from different studies cannot
be placed on an axis like this one.](../figures/fungal-as-ladder.svg){#fig-fungal-ladder width=100%}

Across the kingdom the rate is higher than yeast suggests. A comparative study
of 23 fungi with sampling-depth correction estimated that 6.4 per cent of
annotated fungal genes are alternatively spliced on average, with *Cryptococcus
neoformans* reaching 18 per cent. Basidiomycota averaged 8.6 per cent against
6.0 per cent for Ascomycota, a difference those authors call not significant
[@grutzmann2013fungal].

Within that dataset the rate rises with structural complexity. It runs from 0.26
per cent in the mostly single-celled Saccharomycotina and Taphrinomycotina,
through 2.3 per cent in Mucoromycotina and 7.2 per cent in the filamentous
Pezizomycotina, to 8.6 per cent in the fruiting-body-forming Basidiomycota
[@grutzmann2013fungal]. *Cryptococcus* is intron-rich by any measure, carrying
40,946 introns, with 99.5 per cent of its expressed genes containing at least
one [@janbon2014cryptococcus].

Pathogens remodel their isoform repertoire during infection. Transcriptome data
from the rice blast fungus *Magnaporthe oryzae* spanned vegetative growth and
five stages of rice infection. It yielded 4,270 novel mRNA isoforms from 2,413
genes, 18.1 per cent of the gene set [@jeon2022riceblast].

Some fungi go further and operate the host's splicing machinery directly. The
Glomeromycotina-specific SP7-like effector family of arbuscular mycorrhizal
fungi localises to nuclear condensates. There it binds the plant splicing
factor SR45 together with the core spliceosome proteins U170K and U2AF35.
Expressed in potato, it shifts the host alternative splicing programme
[@betz2024mycorrhizal]. A symbiont establishes itself by changing which isoforms
its host makes.

## Protists and parasites {#sec-protists}

*Plasmodium falciparum* is not the intron-poor organism it is often taken for.
Over half its genes carry predicted introns, and gene-model-independent analysis
of the blood stages added 977 previously undocumented canonical splice
junctions, an 11 per cent increase on the existing annotation
[@sorber2011plasmodium].

*Toxoplasma gondii* shows what the method does to the answer. Junction-level
counting that deliberately ignores intron retention put alternative splicing at
22.6 per cent of annotated genes in uninduced parasites, against roughly 5 per
cent from earlier studies built on reconstructing transcript models. The same
authors note that detection depends heavily on sequencing depth, and that their
own data probably captured well under half of all junctions
[@yeoh2015toxoplasma], and the organism did not change between those two
numbers.

Splicing regulation in the same parasite is a virulence determinant. Deleting
the splicing factor SR2 cut brain cyst burden in infected mice by about 80 per
cent, from roughly 216 cysts per brain in wild type to 46 in the knockout, and
complementation restored the wild-type level [@wu2023sr2].

Ciliates run splicing close to its physical minimum. Every *Paramecium* intron
falls in a narrow 25 to 45 base pair range, among the shortest known, which
those authors read as a functional limit for spliceosomal recognition
[@bondarenko2016ciliate].

Trypanosomes rearranged the problem altogether, and their messenger RNAs were
shown to share an identical 35-nucleotide leader at the 5' end, present on many
and probably all of them [@parsons1984splicedleader]. Genes are transcribed
polycistronically, and individual mature mRNAs are carved out of that transcript
by spliced-leader trans-splicing, obligatorily coupled to cleavage and
polyadenylation in the intergenic regions [@kolev2026transsplicing]. The
splicing reaction there sets transcript boundaries instead of choosing internal
exon content.

## Whether any of this tracks complexity {#sec-trend}

*Chlamydomonas reinhardtii*, which split from land plants around a billion years
ago, gives the green lineage a baseline, showing alternative splicing at 498
transcriptional units and 611 events, about 3 per cent of its gene count
[@labadorf2010chlamydomonas].

A coverage-corrected index built from over 39 million ESTs across 47 sequenced
eukaryotic genomes found alternative splicing rising steadily over roughly 1,400
million years of eukaryotic evolution. Plants scored higher than both fungi and
protists, which those authors read as an independent increase in the plant
lineage rather than a shared trend [@chen2014complexity].

Two things are being measured in all of this, and they move separately. How much
alternative splicing a lineage does is one quantity. Which classes of event it
uses is another, and the switch from cassette exons to intron retention happens
without regard to the first. Any single number offered for an organism is a
property of the assay as much as of the organism. The comparisons that survive
are the ones made inside a single study.
